subject: Biology
title: Sea Otters: Keystone Species
description: Learn Sea Otters: Keystone Species in one minute.

hook.text: When sea otters disappeared from the Pacific coast, entire kelp forests collapsed. Here's why.

buildup.text: Sea otters eat sea urchins. Without otters, urchin populations explode and devour kelp.

discovery.text: Kelp forests shelter hundreds of species and absorb massive amounts of CO₂.

twist.text: Sea otters have the densest fur of any mammal—up to 1 million hairs per square inch—for insulation.

climax.text: Reintroducing otters restored kelp forests within years—proving the power of keystone species.

punchline.text: One small predator holds an entire ecosystem together.

quiz.question: Why are sea otters called a keystone species?
options: Their presence controls urchins and protects kelp forests
They are the largest marine mammal
They build structures other species live in

details.summary: Sea otters are a keystone species whose predation on sea urchins maintains the health of kelp forest ecosystems along the Pacific coast. When otters were hunted to near extinction, urchin populations exploded and destroyed vast kelp forests, creating barren underwater deserts.
details.whyItMatters: The sea otter story is the textbook example of a trophic cascade and keystone species concept. Their recovery shows how protecting a single predator can restore entire ecosystems, providing a powerful conservation lesson.
takeaways: Sea otters control urchin populations preventing kelp forest destruction
Otters were hunted to about 2,000 individuals before protection began
Kelp forests maintained by otters absorb significant carbon and support fisheries

faq.question: How do sea otters maintain kelp forests?
faq.answer: Otters eat sea urchins, keeping their populations in check. Without otter predation, urchins multiply and devour kelp holdfasts, destroying entire forests. Areas with healthy otter populations have lush kelp forests while otter-free areas become barren urchin deserts.

faq.question: Have sea otter populations recovered?
faq.answer: Partially. From a low of about 2,000, southern sea otters number approximately 3,000 today. Northern populations have recovered better in some areas. Threats remain from oil spills, shark predation, and disease. Full recovery to historic numbers is still distant.
